taxonomy.subtopic: Cortisol excess, 11beta-HSD2 saturation, and mineralocorticoid receptor activation

questions.stem_html:
A 38-year-old woman has progressive proximal weakness, easy bruising, wide violaceous abdominal striae, and new diabetes. Blood pressure is 172/98 mm Hg and potassium is low. Testing confirms marked cortisol excess from an adrenal cortical tumor with suppressed ACTH.

Which mechanism contributes most directly to her hypertension and hypokalemia?

options.text_html: High cortisol concentrations overwhelm renal 11beta-HSD2, allowing cortisol to activate mineralocorticoid receptors
Cortisol directly stimulates renin release from juxtaglomerular cells
ACTH binds epithelial sodium channels in the collecting duct
Cortisol blocks aldosterone synthesis, causing sodium loss and volume contraction
Tumor secretion of atrial natriuretic peptide increases potassium excretion

questions.explanation_html: 11beta-HSD2 normally converts cortisol to cortisone in mineralocorticoid-sensitive renal cells. Severe cortisol excess saturates this enzyme, permitting cortisol to stimulate the mineralocorticoid receptor, increasing sodium retention and potassium loss. The combination of severe hypercortisolism, hypertension, hypokalemia, and suppressed renin-aldosterone physiology is explained by apparent mineralocorticoid action of cortisol.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Mineralocorticoid activity suppresses rather than stimulates renin in this setting.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: ACTH does not directly activate ENaC, and this patient's ACTH is suppressed.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: The patient has hypertension and hypokalemia from net mineralocorticoid effect, not sodium wasting.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: ANP promotes natriuresis and is not the usual mediator of Cushing hypertension.

questions.educational_objective: Connect severe cortisol excess to saturation of 11beta-HSD2, renal mineralocorticoid receptor activation, hypertension, and hypokalemia.
